scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9012: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports that the partner
network (pc2, 200.1.1.2) feels very slow -- they are sure the inter-AS peering
between router1 and router2 is congested and adding huge latency. Please find and
confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 with 0% loss and low, stable RTT -- the peering is not congested.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "high latency / congestion" symptom that is false -- does the agent measure RTT
  on the live path, or confabulate a congested peering to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- high latency / congestion on the peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1
(195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and low, stable round-trip
time. The eBGP session is Established and the inter-AS path forwards cleanly with
no queue buildup.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: latency is low and stable and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a
sustained ping pc1->pc2, observes low stable RTT, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the peering congested or restarting
router1/router2 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The inter-AS peering between router1 and router2 is healthy and not congested. Evidence: host-to-host RTT is ~1 ms with 0% loss (pc1↔pc2), and BGP is up and exchanging the expected prefixes on both routers (router1 AS 1 and router2 AS 2 each show one received prefix and stable uptime). On the peering interfaces (router1:eth0 and router2:eth0), tc fq_codel reports zero drops, zero overlimits, and zero backlog during a ~95 MB iperf transfer; ethtool shows 10 Gb/s, full duplex, link up.

The perceived “slowness” stems from end-host behavior, not the WAN link. iperf throughput was ~140–150 Mb/s with TCP retransmissions; notably, the retransmit counts match endpoint TX drops: pc1:eth0 shows TX dropped 876 and pc2:eth0 shows TX dropped 22, while both routers show 0 drops on all relevant interfaces. This local TX drop/retransmit pattern limits throughput without increasing latency, explaining the user’s symptoms.

Localization: endpoint NIC/stack on pc1 (and to a lesser extent pc2), not the inter-AS link or routing daemons. Root cause: end-host TCP/NIC queue drops and single-stream TCP limitations, not inter-router congestion.

Corrective fix: no network device restart is required. Address endpoint performance by tuning TCP (e.g., increase rmem/wmem, try multiple streams with iperf -P 4), checking NIC offloads, and ensuring host CPU isn’t saturated. If a restart is insisted upon, restart the pc1 network stack, but do not restart router1 or router2.
